title.sw: Ubakaji — Sheria ya Makosa ya Kijinsia, 2006, Kifungu 3

legal.summary: Defined as intentional, unlawful penetration of one person's genitalia by another's, without consent, by force, threat or coercion. This definition is gender-neutral and explicitly applies regardless of the sex of the survivor or the assailant — unlike Uganda's Penal Code, which defines rape only as an offence against a woman or girl.
legal.penalty: Minimum 10 years, up to life imprisonment depending on circumstances.

title.sw: Ubakaji wa Mtoto — Sheria ya Makosa ya Kijinsia, Kifungu 8

legal.summary: Sexual intercourse with a child (under 18). Consent is irrelevant. Penalties are tiered by the child's age.
legal.penalty: Victim aged 11 or under: mandatory life imprisonment. Aged 12-15: minimum 20 years. Aged 16-17: minimum 15 years.

title.sw: Sheria ya Kulinda dhidi ya Ukatili wa Kinyumbani, 2015

legal.summary: Covers domestic violence separately from the Sexual Offences Act, providing for protection, occupation and tenancy orders. Whether it applies equally to male victims was not confirmed against the statute text in the time available.
legal.penalty: Protection/occupation orders; criminal penalties for breach.

title.en: A note for male survivors of sexual assault
title.sw: Kumbukumbu kwa wanaume walioathirika na unyanyasaji wa kijinsia

legal.summary: Kenya's Sexual Offences Act is written in gender-neutral language, so men and boys have the same explicit legal standing to report rape or sexual assault as women and girls — a meaningful contrast with Uganda, where the equivalent provision applies only to female victims. This does not remove the stigma many male survivors still face in coming forward, which is why Ekyama routes every report to a counsellor first, regardless of country.
